input:
Students meeting mass transfer for the first time often ask why another dimensionless group is needed, and the Sherwood number answers a practical question: how much does the movement of the fluid actually help? The Sherwood number is defined as the ratio of convective to diffusive mass transfer at a surface. In the numerator stands the rate at which the flowing fluid delivers material to the surface, or carries it away; in the denominator stands the rate at which diffusion alone, acting across a stagnant layer of the same thickness, would transport the material. Because the comparison is made across one and the same layer, the ratio isolates the contribution of the flow itself.

If the value obtained is close to 1, convection is contributing essentially nothing over and above diffusion. The fluid may well be in motion, yet that motion does not thin the layer, and so the transfer is controlled by diffusion across the layer, exactly as it would be in a stagnant film. This limit is the natural benchmark for everything else.

At the other extreme, a large value tells us that convection has taken over. The flow sweeping past the surface maintains only a very thin diffusive layer and constantly renews the fluid in contact with the surface, so that material is transferred far more rapidly than diffusion across the whole layer could achieve, and the observed rate is dictated by the flow pattern and the geometry rather than by the diffusivity alone.

In practice, the Sherwood number earns its keep when a mass-transfer coefficient is required for a geometry and flow arrangement that has never been measured: published correlations give the number in terms of the flow conditions and fluid properties, and the coefficient is back-calculated from it. One caution deserves emphasis: the value is only meaningful together with its basis, since the characteristic length in the definition must match the length used in the correlation, failing which the recovered coefficient will be wrong by the ratio of the two lengths.
target:
The Sherwood number is the ratio of convective to diffusive mass transfer at a surface. The numerator is the rate at which a flowing fluid delivers material to or from the surface; the denominator is the rate at which diffusion alone would move the same material across a stagnant layer of the same thickness. The two rates describe the same transfer across the same layer, so the ratio compares the two mechanisms on one basis, and the comparison is what the number reports.

A value near 1 means that convection adds nothing to the transfer. The fluid may be moving, but its motion does not thin the layer through which the material must diffuse, and diffusion across that layer sets the rate. The stagnant film gives this limit, and the limit is the reference state against which any enhancement by the flow is measured.

A large value means that convection dominates the transfer. Flow past the surface keeps the diffusive layer thin and continually replaces the fluid in contact with the surface, so material crosses far faster than diffusion across the full layer would allow. The rate is then governed mainly by the flow and by the geometry that shapes the flow, and the diffusivity on its own no longer predicts it.

The Sherwood number is used where a mass-transfer coefficient is needed for a geometry and a flow that have not been measured. Correlations report the number as a function of the flow conditions and the fluid properties, and the coefficient is recovered from the number. A reported value is tied to its basis: the length in the definition must be the length the correlation used, or the recovered coefficient is wrong by the ratio of the two lengths.
